Sansec text: the most common pattern puts the shop's product option number in front of index.php (for example 780index.php). The value is a pattern: digits, then index.php

Sansec text: the check value hard-coded in the most common shell, derived from the secret cookie value. It has 42 hex characters, which matches no standard hash length, so it may be a typing slip on Sansec's page. Recorded as written. Confirm with a second source before relying on it
Sansec text: the hard-coded check value (an MD5 of the password, applied twice) in the second shell variant. It is a value inside the file's code, not a hash of the whole file

Sansec text: the number the back door always prints, used by attackers to find live shells. A bare number appears in many pages; the signal is a page that returns only this number from a path that should not exist

value: Any .php, .phtml or .phar file inside the shop's upload folder
notes: Sansec text: a strong indicator of compromise. The folder also holds ordinary uploads, so look at the file types

value: A script file in the upload folder that starts like a GIF or PNG image
notes: Sansec text: attackers upload files that are valid images and also contain PHP code, called polyglots. The most common one starts with a GIF header

value: A file name written with Unicode escape codes that decodes to an ordinary name such as bypass.php
notes: Sansec text: some attackers obfuscate the file name this way

value: An assets/images folder created inside several top-level shop folders, each holding a copy of the back door
notes: Sansec text: the attackers create this subfolder in every top-level folder they can write to, so that one copy survives a cleanup

value: Obfuscated JavaScript added to CMS pages or static blocks that reloads a saved copy from the visitor's browser and fetches a fresh one from an outside site
notes: Sansec text: a two-stage loader. Blocking the outside site does not clear copies already saved in visitors' browsers

value: Requests to the guest shopping-cart routes that carry an embedded file, followed by a new file in the upload folder
notes: Sansec text: the anonymous cart routes are the most dangerous way in. Our note, not Sansec's: request bodies are often not logged, so this may show only as unusual cart requests plus a new file. We left out the exact routes and request layout
